task.goal: Help adult learners recognize misleading averages in a short public-health chart.
hard_constraints: One 50-minute class with 12 learners and printed charts; no internet or personal medical data.
Learners must compare mean and median without assuming prior statistics training.
Check transfer to a new chart and time spent, not just recall of definitions.
task.available_resources: Whiteboard and two anonymized example datasets.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Move one value: make the misleading average visible
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners physically rearrange printed value slips to see how one unusually large observation moves the mean while leaving the median relatively stable. This makes sensitivity to extreme values tangible before introducing terminology.

Prepare a short public-health chart and 12 value slips derived from the first anonymized dataset, preserving a relevant extreme value if one exists. Explain mean as an equal share of the total and median as the middle of an ordered line; demonstrate the even-number case. Learners work in four groups of three, ordering slips and calculating both summaries with guided arithmetic. They then replace the largest value with a clearly labeled hypothetical larger value and predict which summary changes. Groups annotate the chart with what its average reveals and conceals. Explicitly explain that neither summary is automatically misleading: the appropriate choice depends on the question, distribution, and labeling.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; common explanation, 8; assigned activity, 12; discussion, 8; individual transfer assessment, 10; feedback, 8. Keep the second dataset unseen until transfer. Its chart should use a different health measure and scale.

Needs: printed charts, slips, arithmetic scaffolds, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the datasets contain manageable numerical observations. If neither has useful asymmetry, use a labeled hypothetical modification for instruction, while acknowledging that transfer to strongly skewed data remains untested. This lesson addresses distributional distortion, not every possible chart problem.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign two groups to the manipulation activity and two to an equal-length worked example covering the same calculations. Before shared discussion, collect a brief independent explanation; treat the later transfer comparison cautiously because discussion may reduce differences. On the unseen chart, require each learner to calculate or locate mean and median, assess a headline, and explain which summary fits a stated question. Record completion time and unfinished responses at ten minutes. Score calculations and justified interpretation separately. The mechanism is weakened if manipulation produces no clearer explanation of extreme-value effects than the worked example, or only improves answers by requiring substantially more time. With 12 learners, results are descriptive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Audit the headline against the question
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach learners to evaluate an average as evidence for a specific public-health claim. The central action is checking whether a summary answers the question being asked, rather than spotting an unusual number alone.

Use the first dataset to prepare one short chart with its underlying values and two possible headlines: one about a typical observation and one about the total divided across observations. Both must be plausible enough to inspect, without implying either mean or median is always preferable. In four groups of three, learners complete an audit sheet: What is being claimed? What does each observation represent? What is the mean? What is the median? Which headline is supported, and what qualification is needed? Rotate reader, calculator, and challenger roles. Groups then rewrite one headline so its summary and scope are explicit.

Schedule: individual first impression, 5 minutes; plain-language instruction in mean and median, 8; assigned practice, 12; individual transfer, 10; comparison of reasoning, 10; corrective feedback, 5. Introduce the second dataset only during transfer, with a new chart, headline, units, and practical question. Ask learners to accept, qualify, or reject the claim and support their decision numerically.

Needs: printed charts, audit sheets, arithmetic guides, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the datasets have enough context to identify their observational units. Do not invent missing population or sampling information; mark those limits explicitly. This approach may improve claim evaluation while leaving independent calculation fragile, so both require assessment. Avoid teaching a shortcut that ‘typical’ always mandates the median.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign six learners to the audit sheet and six to a conventional calculate-and-define worksheet using the same first dataset and equal practice time. Give everyone identical instruction and the same individual transfer chart before discussion. Score correct mean and median separately from whether the learner connects the chosen summary to the claim and acknowledges a relevant limitation. Record each learner’s completion time, with a ten-minute cap and unfinished work retained. Include one transfer question for which the mean is useful, so blanket rejection of means fails. The audit mechanism is challenged if learners merely repeat cautionary language, cannot justify decisions using the new values, or perform no better than the comparator on claim evaluation. Offer the audit sheet to everyone afterward.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Predict, inspect, and revise a distribution
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: expose the information lost in a single average by asking learners to predict the underlying observations, then compare their predictions with the actual distribution. A mismatch creates a concrete reason to inspect both mean and median.

Start with a printed public-health chart showing only the mean from the first dataset. Ask learners to sketch where they expect individual observations to lie on a supplied number line; stress that several distributions could fit. Reveal the actual anonymized values on a second printed panel. Learners compare their sketches with the observations, order the values, and find the median. Introduce mean as equal sharing and median as the middle position, with a worked example and support for even-sized datasets. In pairs, learners explain what the original chart allowed them to infer and what it left uncertain. They revise its caption or add a small distribution display.

Schedule: prediction, 5 minutes; explanation, 8; assigned inspection activity, 12; individual transfer, 10; discussion and revision, 10; feedback, 5. Use the second dataset for an unseen chart with different units. Its assessment asks learners to distinguish conclusions supported by the mean alone from conclusions requiring the displayed observations, then compare mean and median once the observations are revealed.

Needs: paired printed chart panels, number-line sheets, whiteboard, arithmetic supports, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the source values are available and small enough to inspect on paper. Predictions are hypotheses, not errors to ridicule. The mechanism may be less striking when the first dataset is nearly symmetric; even then, multiple possible distributions remain a valid lesson.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Randomly assign three pairs to predict before seeing the values and three pairs to inspect the same values immediately. Keep numerical instruction, materials, and total practice time equal. Assess transfer individually before group discussion. Score whether learners avoid unsupported claims about most observations, correctly compare mean and median, and use the revealed distribution to justify a conclusion. Record time separately for the mean-only judgment and the subsequent full-data judgment, within the ten-minute assessment window. The prediction step is not supported if it adds time without improving calibrated conclusions relative to immediate inspection, or if learners become indiscriminately distrustful even after adequate data are shown. Treat this small comparison as a classroom feasibility check, not a reliable effect estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repair a plausible mistake before it becomes a rule
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners diagnose and repair incorrect worked solutions. Comparing a plausible error with a correct explanation could help them distinguish arithmetic mistakes from unsupported interpretations, and recognize those errors in a new chart. The active ingredient is explaining why a tempting solution fails.

Prepare a printed public-health chart and underlying observations from the first anonymized dataset. Add two clearly labeled fictional student solutions: one finds the median without ordering the values; another correctly calculates the mean but claims that most observations must equal or exceed it. Supply correct calculations separately for checking. Use actual dataset values; if the second claim happens to be true, explain that the mean alone still cannot establish it.

Use 5 minutes for an initial individual judgment, 8 for instruction, 12 for paired practice, 5 for individual explanation, 10 for unseen transfer, and 10 for discussion and feedback. Explain mean as total divided equally and median as the middle after ordering, including the two-middle-values case. During practice, six pairs identify the first unjustified step, repair it, and write a brief explanation that would help its fictional author. Emphasize that either summary can be useful, depending on the question.

Needs: printed charts, solution sheets, arithmetic guides, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Reserve the second dataset for transfer. Its chart must include sufficient observations to compare both summaries. Missing sampling context remains explicitly unknown. Incorrect examples require prompt correction; learners with fragile arithmetic may otherwise remember the error.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Assign three pairs to error repair and three to correct worked examples with equivalent explanation prompts and equal practice time. Before discussion, assess everyone individually on the second chart without fictional solutions: calculate mean and median, evaluate a claim about most observations, and explain an appropriate use of each summary. Record completion times and unfinished work at ten minutes. Score calculations and justified interpretations separately. The mechanism lacks support if repair learners repeat the planted errors, cannot transfer without error labels, or show no interpretation advantage over correct examples despite taking longer. Twelve learners provide a feasibility check, not a reliable effect estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Choose an average by seeing what a decision costs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: learners compare the consequences of using the mean or median as a planning number. Equal-sharing and typical-observation questions become concrete through two different measures of success: matching the observed total and minimizing total absolute distance from individual observations. This could replace the shortcut “one average is always better” with an understanding of why the question matters.

Use the first anonymized dataset and its public-health chart. Explain mean as total divided by count and median as the middle after ordering, including the even-count case. In four groups of three, learners calculate both using printed arithmetic guides. They then complete two paper challenges: multiply each proposed average by the observation count and compare with the actual total; calculate each observation’s distance from each proposed average and add those distances. Explain that distance means the positive gap, without introducing formal notation. The mean reproduces the total; the median minimizes total absolute distance, although ties are possible.

Groups annotate the chart with one question each summary helps answer and one conclusion the chart cannot establish. Clarify that minimizing numerical distance does not establish the best public-health policy, and a median need not be an observed value.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 4 minutes; instruction, 9; challenges, 14; individual unseen-chart assessment, 10; discussion and feedback, 13.

Needs: printed charts, calculation tables, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Reserve the second dataset for transfer. Assumes manageable numerical values with meaningful totals and differences; inspect this before teaching. Do not relabel observations or invent sampling context. If mean and median coincide, the exercise demonstrates agreement but provides weaker evidence about recognizing misleading averages.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give two groups the consequence challenges and two an equal-duration calculation worksheet with the same instruction. Before shared feedback, assess all 12 learners individually on the second chart: calculate mean and median, select a summary for each of two stated purposes, and judge a claim about typical observations using the displayed values. Record completion minutes and unfinished items at the ten-minute cap. Score arithmetic separately from justified interpretation. The mechanism is challenged if learners can complete the distance table but cannot select and justify summaries on transfer, or gain no interpretive advantage while taking longer. This small comparison assesses feasibility, not a dependable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Provide the calculations; teach the interpretation
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: remove arithmetic as an entry requirement so learners can spend their limited time comparing what mean and median communicate. Recognizing a misleading average need not require calculating it independently.

The instructor prepares a printed chart from each anonymized dataset, with correctly calculated mean and median already labeled. Include the underlying observations, units, and number of observations. Use only context actually supplied. Explain mean as the total shared equally and median as the middle of the ordered observations, demonstrating the even-number case on the whiteboard.

Schedule: initial chart judgment, 5 minutes; explanation, 8; supported comparison, 12; individual transfer, 10; discussion, 10; feedback, 5. During practice, four groups of three trace each supplied summary to the observations and explain why the two numbers agree or differ. Each learner then writes a two-sentence caption explaining what a reader could misunderstand from displaying only one summary. Neither summary is presented as universally preferable.

Reserve the second dataset for an unfamiliar transfer chart. Supply both summaries again, change the chart layout, and ask learners to assess two claims: one concerning an equal-share quantity and one concerning a typical observation. Require numerical justification, rather than definitions.

Needs: printed charts and response sheets, whiteboard, and an instructor timepiece. Assumes the instructor can verify the summaries before class and the datasets support understandable examples. This route teaches interpretation with supplied statistics; it does not establish independent calculation ability. If the datasets show little difference between summaries, teach that agreement also matters rather than manufacture a discrepancy.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor assigns six learners to supplied-summary practice and six to the prior headline-audit approach with guided calculation, using equal practice time. Everyone receives the same supplied-summary transfer assessment. Record individual completion times and score justified interpretations separately from terminology. Stop at ten minutes and retain unfinished responses. Prefer this route only if interpretation improves or comparable interpretation takes less time; abandon the shortcut if learners accept incorrect conclusions merely because numbers are supplied. With 12 learners, treat findings as descriptive.

EXPAND.title: Reconstruct who counts before comparing averages
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: prevent a denominator error upstream of interpretation. Learners discover that averaging subgroup summaries as though every subgroup contained the same number of observations can change the story before the mean-versus-median choice even begins.

The instructor checks whether the first dataset can be partitioned into two unequal-sized groups without inventing population labels. Arbitrary groups may be labeled explicitly as teaching partitions. Prepare a printed chart containing every observation, subgroup counts, subgroup means, and the overall mean and median. Include a deliberately incorrect, clearly identified draft caption that calls the unweighted average of subgroup means the overall mean. Do not imply that subgroup medians can simply be averaged either.

Schedule: opening judgment, 4 minutes; plain-language mean and median instruction, 9; reconstruction in four groups of three, 12; correction discussion, 8; individual transfer, 10; feedback, 7. Groups use tally marks on paper to track how many observations each subgroup contributes. With guided arithmetic, they reconstruct the overall total and count, then order the observations to locate the overall median. They correct the caption and explain which people or observations the original calculation undercounted.

Use the second dataset for an unseen chart with a different partition and layout. Ask learners to distinguish the overall mean, overall median, and average of subgroup means, then evaluate a claim about the whole displayed sample.

Needs: printed charts, tally worksheets, whiteboard, and instructor timing. Requires manageable raw datasets whose unequal partitions produce an instructive difference. If that prerequisite fails, this route is unsuitable. Its scope is aggregation across displayed observations; it cannot justify claims about an unspecified population.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor compares two groups using reconstruction with two using the prior headline-audit worksheet, keeping instruction and practice time equal. On individual transfer, score correct identification of the overall summaries and the denominator mistake. Record completion time and arithmetic errors as a shifted cost. End assessment at ten minutes. Retain reconstruction only if it improves aggregation judgments without materially reducing correct mean-versus-median comparisons. A descriptive first-trial stop rule is to discontinue it if most learners cannot complete the core comparison within the cap.

EXPAND.title: Teach when the chart cannot support a decision
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: train a usable action-versus-handoff rule. A learner should sometimes correct an interpretation immediately and sometimes request missing evidence; guessing a median from a mean-only chart is itself a failure.

Prepare three chart packets from the first dataset. One shows mean, median, and observations. A second, otherwise closely matched packet hides the observations and median. A third changes the layout and withholds a different essential item, such as what each observation represents. Explain mean as equal sharing and median as the ordered middle, including an even-sized example. Learners practice three responses: accept a narrowly supported statement, qualify or correct an unsupported interpretation when enough evidence is available, or request the specific missing information.

Schedule: first judgment, 4 minutes; instruction, 9; paired boundary practice, 12; individual transfer, 10; discussion, 10; feedback, 5. Six pairs examine the close pair. With observations available, they compare mean and median and decide whether the displayed claim is justified. With only the mean available, they identify what cannot be determined and write a bounded replacement statement reporting only what is known. Their request goes to the instructor, who supplies a prepared reveal sheet; learners then revise their decision. This provides a complete recovery path without internet access.

Reserve the second dataset for an unfamiliar transfer case. Its packet requires the same decision rule but changes units, layout, and the missing-information pattern.

Needs: printed packets and reveal sheets, whiteboard, and instructor timing. Assumes the raw datasets have enough documented context to prepare truthful examples. The rule concerns interpreting charts, not making personal medical decisions. Missing evidence warrants a specific limitation, not blanket distrust.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor assigns six learners to boundary practice and six to the prior headline-audit approach. Assess everyone individually using a sufficient/insufficient close pair and one unfamiliar case from the second dataset. Score the action choice, mean-versus-median reasoning, and specificity of any information request. Record completion time and unnecessary requests, since indiscriminate handoff shifts work to others. Stop at ten minutes. Reject this route if it increases requests without reducing unsupported conclusions, or reduces correct decisions on sufficient charts. Report descriptive counts, not an efficacy claim.

EXPAND.title: Headline audit with an arithmetic recovery path
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Audit the headline against the question.” Preserve its claim-focused audit, group roles, headline revision, and individual transfer. Its concrete gap is that unfinished arithmetic can prevent learners from reaching the interpretation the class is intended to teach. Change: the instructor supplies a calculation-recovery strip when a group cannot obtain both summaries after four minutes of practice. The strip gives verified mean and median with the total, count, and ordered middle positions. Learners must trace each number to the observations before resuming the audit. Record recovery use; supplying answers does not establish independent calculation ability.

Prepare printed charts from the two anonymized datasets, showing observations, units, and only documented context. Explain mean as total divided equally and median as the ordered middle, including the even-number case. Four groups of three use the first chart to identify the claim and observational unit, compare both summaries, and rewrite the headline with a justified qualification. Neither statistic is universally preferable.

Timing: initial judgment 5 minutes; instruction 8; group audit 12; individual transfer 10; discussion 10; feedback 5. During transfer, reserve the first three minutes for an unaided comparison, then give everyone a verified-summary strip for the remaining interpretation questions. Collect or mark the initial answers before revealing the strip. This separates calculation difficulty from interpretation without extending the class.

The instructor owns preparation, timed recovery, and feedback. Needs: printed charts, audit sheets, recovery strips, whiteboard, and a classroom clock or instructor timepiece. Before class, verify the summaries and observational units. If context is missing, restrict claims to the displayed observations. If both datasets have similar mean and median, teach their agreement and assess unsupported claims about individual observations rather than manufacture a discrepancy. Expected benefit is more completed claim evaluation; costs are extra printing and possible dependence on supplied calculations. Benefit remains untested.
EXPAND.experiment: In a first class of 12, assign two groups of three to the recovery procedure and two to the source audit without recovery strips during practice; keep practice time equal. All receive the identical individual transfer chart from the second dataset, with a different layout and public-health measure if the supplied materials permit. Include an equal-share claim and a claim about typical observations. Score initial mean–median comparison separately from numerical justification, headline judgment, and a defensible replacement statement after the common reveal. Record recovery use, time to complete, and unfinished answers at ten minutes. The instructor compares descriptive counts and times with the source procedure. Stop the recovery procedure during practice if learners simply copy the strip without tracing its evidence: use the remaining practice time for one instructor-led trace, then resume the audit. Retain the change for later teaching only if more learners reach justified interpretations without a clear increase in unsupported claims or assessment time; twelve learners cannot establish efficacy.

EXPAND.title: Test the claim by counting its counterexamples
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: turn an average-based headline into a directly testable statement about the displayed observations. Learners do not first have to decide which average is best. They test what words such as “most” actually assert, then use mean and median to explain why an average alone might invite the wrong conclusion. This targets the inference from a summary to people or observations, rather than arithmetic, headline rewriting, or missing-information requests as the primary activity.

The instructor prepares a short chart and raw-value table from each supplied dataset. For practice, select a threshold in the measure’s units and explicitly label it as a classroom comparison point, not a medical cutoff. Print two claims about the displayed sample, one supported and one unsupported by counting. Use whichever claims the actual values support; do not fabricate a desired distribution. Learners underline the claim’s quantity word, tally observations on each side of the threshold, and state whether the count supports the claim. Explain that “most” means more than half and distinguish “above” from “at or above.”

Timing: opening chart judgment 4 minutes; plain-language instruction on mean and median, including an even-sized example, 9; instructor demonstration of claim counting 5; practice in six pairs 10; individual transfer 10; discussion and corrective feedback 12. Supply verified mean and median alongside the observations. During practice and transfer, require learners to compare the two values and explain whether either value alone establishes the proposed count. Include a separate equal-share question for which the mean answers the question directly, preventing blanket rejection of means.

The instructor owns threshold selection, verification, and correction. Needs: printed charts, tally sheets, whiteboard, and instructor timing. Reserve dataset two for transfer with a different chart layout and threshold. If a dataset has too few distinct values for a useful supported/unsupported claim pair, use claims about exact counts or all observations; explicitly limit what this tests about majority claims. If counting stalls, the instructor models one tally during practice and learners finish the remainder. The likely cost is additional counting; this route addresses claims about displayed observations and does not justify population or medical conclusions.
EXPAND.experiment: For a bounded first trial, give three pairs the claim-counting practice and three pairs an equal-length supplied-summary interpretation worksheet using the same dataset and common mean–median instruction. Assess everyone individually on the unseen second chart before discussion. Include one supported and one unsupported claim about counts, a mean-versus-median comparison, and an equal-share question. Require counts or numerical evidence, not definitions. The instructor records completion times, unfinished responses at ten minutes, tally errors, unsupported conclusions, and inappropriate rejection of the mean. Compare justified decisions and time burden descriptively. Stop adding tally exercises if most learners cannot finish the first practice claim within five minutes; use the remaining practice time to model its count and connect it to the summaries. Do not adopt the route if improved count judgments come with substantially poorer mean–median comparison or persistent failure to complete transfer. No superiority is assumed before this check.
